With ninety students in the first-year architecture studio and only three weeks left in the semester, Professor Lalit Kumar had little time for anyone. But he noticed Chaitanya.
Every other student pinned rough sketches on the review wall; Chaitanya pinned nothing until the final, immaculate board. On Tuesday, when a jury member gave his model 8 out of 10 for a slightly uneven roof, Chaitanya walked out, and Lalit found him crying on the stairs.
That evening Lalit changed his plan. At Wednesday's studio he pinned up his own first sketch for a housing project from years ago: crooked lines, a staircase going nowhere. "This got me a grumpy review," he said. Then he announced a new rule: every student pins a messy sketch by Friday, marked only for effort.
Chaitanya hesitated at the wall for a long time before pinning a pencil drawing with visible erasures. Lalit stopped beside it. "Brave. I like the second window idea."

qa.q: What mark did the jury give Chaitanya's model?
qa.a: 8 out of 10, for a slightly uneven roof.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have hesitated so long at the wall on Friday?
qa.a: Pinning a sketch with visible erasures felt risky for someone who only shows immaculate work, so he was likely afraid of being seen as less than perfect.

qa.q: What did Lalit do that helped, despite the big class and little time?
qa.a: He showed his own flawed early sketch, made messy drafts a rule marked for effort, and praised Chaitanya's courage and an idea rather than polish.

qa.q: What might other students have felt seeing their professor's crooked old sketch?
qa.a: They may have felt relieved and amused, and more willing to pin their own rough work without fear.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a student who never shows drafts and cries over a small mark, and easing the fear by sharing his own mistakes and allowing messy first tries.

passage:
In Naveen Reddy's English class at a college in Himayatnagar, Farhan's essays always arrived on the final day, never a draft before, and they were almost always the best in the room. Last week Farhan got 17 out of 20 and asked to leave the room. Naveen saw him later near the bike stand, eyes red, staring at the paper as though it said 2.
On Monday Naveen brought his own notebook to class, one from his twenties, full of poems with lines struck out and a publisher's rejection slip tucked inside. "I still keep this," he said. "Mistakes are how the good lines got found."
Then he set a new task: a rough, messy draft by Wednesday. "I'll only comment on what you tried, not give a mark."
Farhan's draft came in on Wednesday night, clearly untidy. Naveen wrote back: "Good effort on the argument. Keep going."
The next morning Farhan stayed after class to ask a question.

qa.q: What was tucked inside Naveen's old notebook?
qa.a: A publisher's rejection slip.

qa.q: What might Naveen have felt seeing Farhan near the bike stand with red eyes?
qa.a: He was likely concerned to see a strong student crushed by 17 out of 20, which is why he changed his approach on Monday.

qa.q: Which of Naveen's steps might reduce Farhan's fear, and why?
qa.a: Showing his own struck-out poems and rejection slip, and asking for a messy draft with comments only on effort, make mistakes seem normal and safe.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt receiving 'Good effort on the argument. Keep going.'?
qa.a: He may have felt relieved that an untidy draft brought encouragement instead of judgement, which could be why he stayed to ask a question.

grounding: Illustrates a lecturer who notices a student who never submits drafts and is crushed by a small mark, and responds with his own flawed work and effort-based comments.

"Varun, stay a minute?"
"Yes, ma'am."
"You haven't turned in a single draft this term. Only finals."
"The drafts aren't good enough to show."
"And on Tuesday, you cried over a seven out of ten."
Varun went red. "It should have been ten."
Rajni ma'am pulled out a folder. "This is my PhD chapter. See the comments? 'Unclear.' 'Rewrite.' 'Weak argument.'"
"That's yours?"
"Mine. Messy first tries are how everyone learns. Next week, bring me a messy draft. I'll grade only the effort."
Varun looked at the red comments for a long time. "Okay, ma'am."

qa.q: What mark did Varun cry over?
qa.a: Seven out of ten.

qa.q: What was Rajni ma'am feeling as she pulled out her folder?
qa.a: Rajni ma'am seemed concerned and caring, wanting Varun to see that mistakes are normal.

qa.q: Why is Rajni ma'am's approach likely to reduce Varun's fear?
qa.a: Showing her own corrected work and allowing a messy draft graded only on effort makes imperfection feel safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Varun to see his teacher's red comments?
qa.a: Varun seems surprised and thoughtful, perhaps relieved that even teachers get corrected.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a student who never hands in drafts and cries over a small mark, and sharing her own mistakes to ease his fear.

passage:
Looking back at my first year teaching, the student I remember most is Pema. She never submitted drafts. Only final essays, polished to a shine. When she got a B+ on one, she cried in the corridor.
At first I praised her perfection. "Flawless again, Pema!" I thought I was helping.
Then I saw her face when she got that B+. Fear, not disappointment.
So I changed. I started praising effort: "I can see how hard you worked on this argument." I showed the class my own essay from college, with my professor's comments. And I made first drafts count for marks only if they were messy.
By the end of term, Pema handed me a draft with crossings-out. I nearly cried myself. I'm Vidya, and I still teach that way.

qa.q: What mark made Pema cry in the corridor?
qa.a: A B+.

qa.q: What was Vidya feeling on seeing Pema's face after the B+?
qa.a: Vidya felt worried and troubled, seeing fear rather than disappointment, and realised the praise for perfection was feeding it.

qa.q: Which of Vidya's changes helped Pema?
qa.a: Praising effort, showing Vidya's own corrected college essay, and rewarding messy first drafts.

qa.q: What was it like for Pema to hand in a draft with crossings-out?
qa.a: Pema was likely nervous but brave, trusting that mess would be accepted.

grounding: Shows a teacher recalling a student who never submitted drafts and cried over a small mark, and changing to praise effort and messy tries.

Teacher's note, October
Francis, second-year history, has not submitted a single draft this term, only final essays. His work is excellent. But on Monday, after getting 17 out of 20, he stayed behind and cried. He said, "I should have got full marks. I'm not good at this."
I am worried he connects his worth to every mark.
I have made three changes. I now praise effort and specific progress in his feedback. I showed the class a draft of my own with my editor's comments. And for the next essay, drafts are required and marked only for trying.
Today he submitted a rough draft. It had a question mark in the margin. Small step.
Chetan

qa.q: What mark did Francis get on Monday?
qa.a: 17 out of 20.

qa.q: What is Chetan worried about?
qa.a: Chetan feels worried that Francis ties his worth to every mark.

qa.q: Which changes did Chetan make, and why might they help?
qa.a: Praising effort, showing a personal draft with an editor's comments, and requiring drafts marked only for trying, which make mistakes feel safe.

qa.q: What might Francis be feeling as he hands in a rough draft?
qa.a: Francis is probably nervous, but slightly braver, trying something that isn't perfect.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a student who never submits drafts and cries over a small mark, and making changes to reduce the fear.

Thursday.
Third week as a TA, and I think I've found my hardest case: Imran, first year, clearly the sharpest in the lab section. He has never once submitted a draft for feedback. Today he got 17 out of 20 on the circuits report, the top mark, and I saw him in the corridor afterwards wiping his eyes. He said, "I lost three marks on the diagram. I should have redone it."
I remembered being exactly like that in first year.
So in the next section I did something unplanned. I put my own old second-year report on the projector, red pen all over it, and said, "This is what my drafts looked like. Drafts are supposed to be ugly." A few people laughed. Imran didn't, but he stayed back and asked, "Anirban sir, can I send you a rough version next week?" I said yes, and that I'd comment on his thinking, not his neatness.

qa.q: What mark did Imran get on the circuits report?
qa.a: 17 out of 20, the top mark.

qa.q: Why did Anirban put the old report on the projector?
qa.a: He recognised his own first-year fear in Imran and felt moved to show that drafts are supposed to be ugly.

qa.q: What makes Anirban's response likely to help Imran?
qa.a: Showing a marked-up draft of his own and promising feedback on thinking, not neatness, makes a messy first try feel safe.

qa.q: What is it like for Imran to lose three marks?
qa.a: For Imran it feels like a failure worth crying over, even with the top mark, because the diagram wasn't perfect.

grounding: Shows a tutor noticing a student who never submits drafts and cries over a small mark, and easing the fear by sharing their own mistakes.
